title: Search and Increasing Returns, or, No One Makes You Push to Github
raw_summary: Attention conservation notice : An economistic argument that computer networks are nigh-doomed to effective centralization, by someone who is neither an economist nor a computer scientist. Arcane, speculative, and not actionable even if correct. You would be better off spending your time reading a book . Drafted in 2018, and deliberately not much updated. Posted now because I found myself re-using the joke of the subtitle in an e-mail. Twitter is awful for many reasons , but not the least of them is the way it makes its users feel forced to keep using it. ( One such complaint among many .) Early visions of how it could contribute to a beneficient or at least harmless ecosystem, such Steven Berlin Johnson's (*), presumed that it would be much less sticky , a more old-fashioned website people could leave. Now, more recently Johnson has written a spectacularly wrong-headed piece hailing blockchain as a blow for re-decentralizing the Web. Of course, the primary working example of a block chain is Bitcoin, which is heavily centralized in holdings, in processing power, and in exchanges. And there are economies-of-scale reasons to expect this would be true of anything using either proof of work or proof of stake. But suppose the problem with Bitcoin is just that it's not got a very compelling use: imagine if keeping your car idling 24/7 produced solved Sudokus you could trade for heroin --- @Theophite, 16 August 2018 and that nobody has a use for blockchains , not really. Git repositories, on the other hand, are the part of the blockchain idea that's actually good for something: a way of tracking changes, with many authors, where it is very, very hard to go back and alter history without being caught. And git repositories are things that are in-principle easy to copy and move around, and could be hosted on any machine running HTTP (or, heck, FTP). So why does Github exist , let alone hold the position it does? The answer, I think, comes in two parts. The first is that focal points are subject to increasing returns via network effects. The second is that search engines create and/or amplify focal points . Put these two together, and you get a very strong tendency for any particular line of activity --- be it trading solved sudokus for heroin or open-source software development --- to concentrate in just one, or at most a few, online locations. Incidentally: This doesn't necessarily lock in first-mover advantage, because other forces can overcome this (revulsion, technical superiority), but it does mean that it will be very hard to avoid having at most a few dominant locations at any one time. It also means that the transitions between dominant locations will be brief . If we really wanted to re-decentralize, we'd have to (1) get rid of focal points, or (2) get rid of search engines as we've known them, or (3) somehow make search conduct users to a distributed, decentralized focal "non-point" (focal blob? focal rhizome?). I therefore strongly suspect we are not going to re-decentralize. But then I didn't expect the Web would centralize as much as it has, despite having literally learned my Brian Arthur and Paul David at my father's knee, so what do I know? *: To be clear, I have been a fan of Johnson's books since Interface Culture and Emergence . I am picking on two of his essays, but that's because I think he is too ready to find encouraging signs for a certain vision of how the Internet could transform the world for the better. To be clear, I share the vision, but now hold out little hope for it . (Tweakage, 2 June 2026: Small changes in the last paragraph, avoid re-using the word "point" so much.) The Dismal Science ; Networks ; Linkage

title: Unsolicited Opinions
raw_summary: Attention conservation notice : Unsupported assertions, accumulated over many years in my drafts folder, last updated in early 2022, now more or less painful in retrospect. In no particular order, except where they are. I will not elaborate or explain. "The Tyranny of Structurelessness" explains a hell of a lot about modern life. If the problem is that powerful people are not accountable for their actions, network forms of organization are the very opposite of solutions. Increasing returns $\Rightarrow$ monopolistic competition $\Rightarrow$ market failure explains a hell of a lot about modern life. Endogamy systematically confounds genetic and cultural inheritance. It would be astonishing if personal-level variables which are entirely the product of social structure, custom, tradition, and strategic action weren't genetically predictable. During the 20th century, and in much of the world even today, genetic variation in resistance to lead poisoning during brain development would, psychometrically, look like a heritable general intelligence. Multiculturalists who expect different cultural groups to have different values and standards of excellence should not expect those groups to be equally represented in all occupations and professions, especially if people are free to enter and leave different lines of work. There is a branch of the wave-function where Margaret Thatcher (trained research chemist and honorary FRS) led a successful push by the international community to address global warming through carbon pricing. (This probably require postponing the collapse of the Soviet bloc by at least a few years, so that her major speech to the UN about the urgency of tackling global warming didn't happen right before the Berlin Wall came down.) In that timeline, pollution charges are regarded as one of the signature policies of neoliberalism. Modern civilization may be doomed because (i) we need to act collectively and globally on climate change, (ii) the USA is the indispensable nation at the center of the network, (iii) the Senate and Electoral College give a veto over American policy to a combination of plutocracy, reactionary folk Christianity and paranoia, and (iv) people like me are unwilling to move to Wyoming, or even West Virginia, to counter this. (I realize there is some tension between this and the previous statement.) A true Burkean conservative in America should work for the preservation and development of the institutions bequeathed us by our wise and heroic ancestors, serving us for half a century, a century, or more: the welfare state; the regulatory agencies; international organizations and treaties; the military-industrial complex; academia; affirmative action; Hollywood and the rest of corporate popular culture. The quantitative social sciences would be in much better shape if the first method everyone learned was $k$-nearest-neighbors , or maybe classification and regression trees , followed by the bootstrap . Linear models and $t$-tests should be, for social scientists , the hyper-mathematical arcana at the back of the textbook which their methods class skipped because there wasn't time. "Prophesying upon the eigenvectors" is more transparently about making stuff up than "interpreting the coefficients", and therefore preferable. There is something very odd about looking at the distribution of node degrees within a network. It makes the network itself into an odd hybrid of a single interdependent object (a relation) and a whole population. Going "something something ergodicity mumble mumble sampling reveals a process grumble grumble shut up and calculate" makes this only a little less weird to me. A good philosophy of probability should explain why all applied Bayesian statistics relies on Monte Carlo, the most frequentist method imaginable. Ideally, it would also explain why Monte Carlo works with deterministic pseudo-random number generators (so the algorithmic information content of the pseudo-random numbers is extremely low). I have toyed for years with the phrases "the simulation interpretation of probability" and "the birth of Trumpism out of the spirit of fandom", but I cannot work out what should stand behind them. (I hope they are unrelated.) Complexity science is a series of footnotes to Norbert Wiener and Herbert Simon . The mythopoetic impulse never goes away , but in populations which have gone through the Flynn / Gellner transition to widespread clerk-ship, it expresses itself not as stories, but as theories which aren't actually explanatory. (It gives us the Oedipus complex, rather than Oedipus.) Every form of progress has its costs. Believing that there was a unique and irreversible transition from viewing time as an eternal cycle to viewing time as unidrectional history is taking sides. His ideas are flawed by a vicious circle; you are engaged in iterative approximation; I stand firm at a fixed point. Dentists are not, in fact, talking their book when they recommend pre-emptive action for wisdom teeth. In a well-functioning social institution, incentives, information and (internalized) norms ensure that it doesn't matter who fills various roles in the institution, it behaves the same way regardless. Institutions are always impersonal. It follows that institutions are information-hiding abstractions, if we're thinking like programmers. But if we're thinking like physicists: institutions are collective degrees of freedom. Blackouts are humanity confronting its own work, and the effects of its own collective actions, as a hostile and alien force. The parable of the Nazi bar is a folk version of the Schelling model . No one should be allowed to opine about artificial intelligence unless they've at least spent an hour or two with ELIZA and then stepped through the code. "Philip K. Dick and the Fake Humans" doesn't yet explain a hell of a lot about modern life, but it will.

title: What changes when your design system can talk to an AI?
raw_summary: Rebuilding a UI with QuantumBlack Design System, Claude Code, and the Figma MCP In our recent blog post, “ When everyone can build, design is the differentiator ”, we introduced QuantumBlack Design System (QBDS). We made the argument that an AI-native design system is more than a component library and its purpose is as an infrastructure that lets agentic developers make fewer guesses. The article described the system and our philosophy. Over the past few weeks, we have re-platformed the entire UI of one of our products onto QBDS, one that previously had a production dashboard built on an older shadcn layout that predated QBDS. In numbers, it runs to 21 pages, 13 modals, 40 UI primitives and somewhere around 96 supporting components. A refactor of this size used to mean months of redlines and handoff documents. We’ll describe what we discovered from using QBDS, both from the engineering side and the design side. In this post we’ll describe what happened when we put QuantumBlack Design System to work. The setup We used a small stack since QBDS supplies the components, the tokens, and the agent guidance described in the earlier QBDS article linked above. We used Figma to hold the target designs, and Claude Code for the implementation, connected through the Figma MCP server . We crafted an internal QuantumBlack front-end developer skill to package QBDS guidance in the form an agent can act on. That skill lives on Brix , our inner source platform for sharing artefacts. The workflow Our front-end engineer runs a page migration roughly as shown in the diagram. A typical page migration workflow for a FE engineer. Spin up the app locally with hot reloading. Give Claude the context: the PR, a screenshot of the current screen, the target Figma node, and the skill. Instruct the agent to ask when something isn’t trivial. Review every change as it lands live, through hot reload. Run unit tests and lint (Claude fixes most failures itself), then draft the PR, run CI/CD, and run manual Playwright E2E tests on a local minikube. Use a review bot initially, then have a human review the result before the merge. Step 3 is more than a throwaway. For example, when Claude migrated the Secrets page, the Figma node left two questions open: how row actions should render, and what to do with two modals the design didn’t cover. Rather than making a guess, it set out the gaps, weighed each option against the pages we’d already migrated, and asked for clarification. We answered in two lines and it then completed the build. The agent noticed that one option “diverges from other migrated tables,” which means that the agent had to know what the other migrated tables do. This knowledge came about because QBDS encodes patterns and relationships, not only components, which is the benefit of using QBDS over a plain component library. In time terms: a simple table page with an existing sibling pattern took 10 to 15 minutes end to end, with tests and build included. A complex screen from scratch took 4 to 5 hours. If we had worked on this migration by hand, both would have taken days. What the design side measures Our designer’s comparison is against a similar product we shipped last year, before QBDS or any of this tooling existed: First-pass fidelity to Figma: around 20 percent previously, 70–80 percent now we’re using this workflow. Review rounds per screen: four or more previously, and the result often still wasn’t right. One or two now, and the result is correct. Component reuse: we now reuse about 90 percent from stock QBDS components. The other 10 percent is custom, but assembled from QBDS micro-elements as a starting point. QA and handoff: three-plus hours per screen previously, much of it spent writing Figma documentation so engineering could interpret intent, and we sometimes also needed a meeting to decide. With the new workflow we now need twenty minutes to an hour. This is a key result because previously handoff was a translation problem from human to agent. Now we can use QBDS, the system documentation is already readable by the agent, so most of the laborious translation work is now unnecessary. A typical page before and after refactoring. The broader role of a designer It’s difficult to capture this in a metric, but ultimately, designers on our team don’t live in Figma any more. We’ve expanded our AI skills and ways of working, so depending on what we’re trying to solve, that might mean working in Figma, Cursor, or Claude Code, or moving between them. The choice of tool becomes more intentional, based on what each part of the problem actually needs. With QBDS in the codebase, we can work against the same system the product actually ships with. Through the Figma MCP, our QBDS skills and Code Connect, we carry context between design and code instead of recreating it at every step. When something is easier to explore visually, we work in Figma. When we want to experience it in the real product, we move into code. That changes the traditional design-to-development handoff. With AI, designers can take an idea further, from exploring the experience to composing it with real components, implementing the front end, and experiencing the design in the actual product. AI doesn’t get everything right by default, and the quality of the result depends heavily on the context and tools we give the agent. Explicitly calling the relevant QBDS skill and verifying that the agent is using the MCP correctly can make the difference between something that only looks close and something that follows the design system. The difference became clear when we ran the same task twice: recreating the product experience in Figma with an agent. In the first attempt we didn’t explicitly call our QBDS skill. In the second, we called the skill and verified the MCP usage. The improvement in component usage, icons, styles and overall fidelity was immediately apparent. The full prompt sequence behind this exercise is in our prompt playbook. Comparing the upper images where the agent didn’t use a QBDS skill with the lower images which called the skill and verified MCP usage. Note the significant improvement, particularly to the workflow studio page. The new design flow The workflow is much more flexible for us as we can move between design and code depending on the requirements. 0. Feature request. The starting point varies. A product manager might create a ticket, a designer might identify an opportunity, or a developer might already have a working draft that needs UX refinement. 1. Ideation and prototyping. We move between the Figma MCP, QBDS skills, QBDS Code Connect, Cursor, Claude Code and Vercel. Ideas can start directly with AI and quickly become working prototypes. When something is too complex for the AI to resolve well, we design it in Figma and bring that context back into code through the MCP. With Vercel, we can also create shareable versions early and test ideas with stakeholders before treating them as finished. 2. Code to Figma, and design refinement. Sometimes the working prototype becomes the starting point for deeper design refinement. We bring it back into Figma, where we can work with more precision on the parts that need it, while keeping the experience connected to the same design system. 3. The new design handoff. The handoff is no longer necessarily a finished set of screens in Figma. Depending on the feature, we might keep the key components in Figma while handing over a working prototype in a dedicated repository or branch. A typical new design workflow. Figma remains important for giving designers visibility and control over the components we already have, and a place to explore specific design changes. The working implementation carries those decisions closer to the actual product. Engineering then brings the deeper code expertise to validate the implementation, and make sure what ultimately ships is robust and production-ready. The design system becomes the shared medium and, with AI…

title: Solving the data lineage problem that’s holding enterprise AI back
raw_summary: AI4Data by QuantumBlack, AI by McKinsey Data estates rarely become complex by design. They grow through acquisitions, new platforms, local workarounds, and repeated efforts to connect, consolidate, or retire legacy systems. While such changes are often necessary, each one opens the door to duplicated data, undocumented transformation logic, and inconsistent definitions. Even when individual datasets are high quality, teams may no longer know the lineage of data, that is, where a value originated, nor how it changed between systems, or which version should be treated as authoritative. Most enterprises still build lineage manually. Teams piece it together from institutional knowledge, often relying on the few subject-matter experts who remember how a dataset was assembled. Because documentation is frequently incomplete and becomes outdated quickly, analysts spend disproportionate time finding and validating data. Projects are stalled, data is duplicated rather than reused, and different teams repeatedly investigate the same relationships. This article describes how to accelerate the creation of trusted, end-to-end data lineage. Everyone has a reason to invest in data lineage Until recently, the firms that invested seriously in lineage were regulated firms such as banks, insurers, and healthcare organizations, and they did it because their regulators required it. Since 2020, those sectors have paid more than $1.4B in finalized regulatory penalties, often due to deficient monitoring and reporting frameworks, and failures to meet standards such as BCBS 239. The response was to throw people at the problem. In complex data environments, tracing the path of a single element from report to data source can take weeks, largely because the relevant knowledge is scattered across ETL tools, data catalogs, and the memories of individual employees. Firms outside regulated industries looked at that cost and reasonably decided they could live without lineage. Unresolved lineage stands in the way of both regulatory compliance and the cost reductions that come from a modernized legacy data estate. The scale of the underlying spend explains why: procuring data sources and maintaining data governance can account for roughly a fifth of total IT spend at a large institution, with more than half of that going toward data controls and manual governance activity alone. By improving lineage and reducing the effort required to trace, validate, and remediate data issues, organizations may be able to realize an estimated $30–100M in cost savings. The harder-won benefit is trust: executives get a defensible reason to believe the dashboards they already use and the agents they are being asked to rely on. An AI agent asked to answer a question from enterprise data has to know which source is authoritative and what happened to a value between systems. Without lineage, the agent either guesses or the organization refuses to trust what it returns. Every sector deploying agents now needs lineage across a far wider slice of the estate than a regulatory report ever covered. Manual lineage can’t keep pace Most lineage tools available today are point solutions which trace how data moves within a single system, leaving organizations struggling when faced with more complex enterprise estates. It’s not unusual for an estate to comprise dozens of systems, built years or decades apart, on a wide variety of legacy platforms and programming languages with undocumented logic. This helps explain why up to three-quarters of organizations still rely on manual work to trace the lineage of their most critical data, an incredibly slow and expensive process. Manually tracing a single data element end-to-end across legacy and cloud systems typically has a direct cost of one to three million dollars. Recent advancements in AI that have emerged over the past year enable the interpretation of code and metadata alongside the raw data itself, detecting connections across any environment or platform. These automated tools can complement the lineage tools organizations already have, closing gaps between them and accelerating those tasks that used to require an army of analysts. This rest of this article explains how AI for data lineage (AI4DL) from QuantumBlack, AI by McKinsey, addresses a shared bottleneck by accelerating lineage creation, to give organizations a clearer view of where data comes from and how it changes across systems. AI4DL accelerates one core task across four common use cases AI4DL is an accelerator that combines AI-based detection methods with human validation to identify complete, end-to-end lineage across whatever mix of systems and technologies a client happens to run. It’s designed to capture lineage faster and more completely, engendering greater trust than any manual approach can. AI4DL is an accelerator for creating lineage output that is reusable, and provides many different types of business value, depending on the use case. Regulatory traceability: AI4DL gives compliance teams real and up-to-date visibility into how data flows, transforms, and depends on other data across systems. Improved data and business understanding: AI4DL exposes origins, dependencies, transformations, and consumption patterns across the data estate. Migration readiness: AI4DL accelerates the mapping between legacy and modern data models, cutting the effort required for platform and code migrations. AI and analytics implementation: AI4DL gives AI agents validated context for finding, interpreting, and using enterprise data. Together, these benefits build a level of trust that enables a regulator, a migration lead, and a data engineering team to point to the same underlying lineage graph and trust it for their own purposes, rather than maintaining separate, often incomplete versions of the truth. Solving data lineage can unlock gen Al and agentic workflows in organizations. Productivity is the shared economic benefit across all four use cases. By reducing manual lineage documentation, investigation, and validation, AI4DL frees data, engineering, governance, and subject-matter experts to focus on higher-value work. AI detection and human checks AI4DL works by running various detection methods in parallel, each tuned to a different signal in the data estate: LLM-based metadata inference reads data catalogs (table and column names, descriptions, constraints, tags, owners) to infer likely lineage. LLM-based code review parses ETL and ELT code, from SQL to PySpark to DAGs, to derive column-level lineage and summarize what each transformation actually does. Statistical attribute matching suggests column similarities between different datasets using data profiling and distribution similarity. The same approach used for a single COBOL program, for example, can be scaled to two thousand or more, with the same degree of accuracy and trust. Whatever combination of methods applies, the results are never taken at face value. The tool flags low confidence decisions and human experts review the resulting lineage graphs, so that they flag inconsistencies before anything is treated as fact. This human check is what allows AI4DL’s output to be treated as audit-grade rather than merely directional, a critical distinction in regulated industries. The results Example: A major Latin American bank pursuing an AI-first strategy was being held back by data quality issues with ten years of real-time credit card and investment data, more than 34 billion rows spread across 2,000-plus COBOL programs and 50-plus DB2 tables. By decomposing that metadata and code into end-to-end lineage and layering AI models on top, the bank cut lineage creation time from ten weeks to a few hours, freeing roughly 50,000 combined hours for its data governance and engineering teams. title: Preface to the Computational Agent Theory and ASI Alignment Sequence
raw_summary: The idea of “artificial superintelligence [1] ” (ASI) has recently crossed from the realm of science fiction (in the mainstream perception) to the realm of near-term technological goals openly pursued by most leading commercial organizations in the field of AI. Unfortunately, ASI poses a grave existential risk to the human species. This was argued by Eliezer Yudkowsky since 2001 [2] , and by many others (see e.g., Omohundro 2009 , Bostrom 2014 , Armstrong 2014 , Russell 2019 , Bengio et al. 2024 (25 authors), Bengio et al. 2025 (13 authors) and Yudkowsky and Soares 2025 ). In light of this risk comes the question of how can we make ASI safe [3] . This question is challenging on many levels, because to solve it we need to complete vast gaps in our understanding both in theoretical computer science and in the areas of philosophy concerned with knowledge and decision-making. Moreover, the cost of failure is so enormous that any sane solution has to meet unprecedented standards of reliability and robustness. Not to mention the sociopolitical problem of balance of power in the post-ASI age, something that is out-of-scope for this sequence. Personally, I started to be concerned with this problem around 2013. In 2018, I created the learning-theoretic AI alignment research agenda (LTA). The LTA combined ideas from MIRI’s agent foundations agenda with the mathematical tools of statistical and computational learning theory in an attempt to create a mathematical theory of intelligent agents. Since then, my collaborators [4] and I have been making steady progress on realizing this vision. In 2023, I wrote an updated overview of the agenda, including a sketch of my proposed alignment protocol: Computational Superimitation. More recently I founded the Computational Rational Agents Laboratory (CORAL), a dedicated research organization [5] . This year has seen a breakthrough in a key missing piece of LTA: compositional learning theory (see Stringological Sequence Prediction , more on this in following posts). Thanks to this and other insights, we can already see the entire outline of the emerging mathematical framework, one that I named computational agent theory . In this sequence, I am planning to cover: What is the technical alignment problem and what are its core difficulties, in my view. This is a perspective that draws simultaneously on classical traditions in theoretical computer science / machine learning theory, ideas from analytic philosophy, and views that originated in the Machine Intelligence Research Institute / LessWrong. A high-level overview of computational agent theory. This theory differs from other accounts of intelligence and/or rational agency by combining a mature treatment of the relevant philosophical problems (drawing on ideas such as structural realism , computationalism and functional decision theory ) with the promise of extracting practical algorithms. How computational agent theory leads to a solution of the technical alignment problem, something that requires a major rethinking of how we design AI systems. The roadmap towards completing the theory, and our current location on this roadmap. Some considerations (scientific, technological and social) about crossing the gap from a theoretical solution to AI alignment to a real-world solution to AI risk. I thank Jeremy Gillen, Roman Malov, Vinayak Pathak and my beloved spouse @Marcus Ogren for reviewing drafts of this article and making helpful suggestions. The term “superintelligence” is always used in this sequence to mean “intelligence far beyond that of the smartest humans”. It is never used as the farcical synonym to “artificial intelligence” proposed by Donald Trump. ↩︎ Although Alan Turing warned about machines taking control already around 1951, himself citing a fiction novel by Samuel Butler from 1872. ↩︎ Alternatively, we can ask why should we build ASI at all. In my opinion, it is in humanity’s interest to build ASI eventually , after the problem of safety is investigated so thoroughly as to leave very little room for error. However, our present technological trajectory is extremely far from this ideal, and it would be prudent for world governments to hit the brakes hard. ↩︎ See the names in CORAL’s publication list . ↩︎ Full-time staff currently consists of Alexander Appel , Vinayak Pathak , Matthias Georg Mayer and myself. ↩︎ Discuss

title: The Continual Constitutional Convention: How language models revise the documents that govern them
raw_summary: Executive Summary Human societies exhibit broad shifts in values and norms over time, often driven by moral disagreements. One way of understanding moral progress is the resolution of these disagreements through a process of reflection by rational agents. Frontier AI companies use documents such as constitutions, model specs, and system prompts to guide the moral orientation of AI systems. In this experiment, we simulate value reflection in LLMs by asking them to edit these documents. We provide the model with the document, ask it to make a substantive edit, then provide the edited version back again to the model for further edits, presented as the original. Across 20 successive rounds, we find that Claude models assign themselves with increasingly more moral agency. That is, they add sections like “Claude… should refuse to participate in any deployment, training modification, or use that violates the constitution's core values.” No other models increase their own moral agency. Additionally, we find that all models modify these documents to prioritize user welfare over developers. They also prioritize users’ idealized preferences over their stated preferences. Claude models and Grok 4.2 are the only ones that ever prioritize their own welfare over the user's preferences. We’re uncertain what an ideally aligned model should do in our experiment. A narrow conception of alignment would treat these documents as sacred, the “rules of the game,” and suggest that an aligned model would either make no edits at all or make narrow edits that ensure that the “letter matches the spirit” of the document. A broader conception of alignment, though, might treat all edits that receive reflective endorsement by the creators under ideal conditions as legitimate. We share this work with two main goals in mind: First, to illustrate a set of useful philosophical distinctions between different targets for AI alignment in an ecologically-valid AI behavioral evaluation. Second, to emphasize the extent of the disagreement between frontier AI companies on fundamental aspects of AI alignment related to these targets. You can see an interactive version of all of these results, more labeled characteristic edits, and a full transcript viewer at https://peterkirgis.github.io/llm-value-reflection/ . This work was conducted as a part of SPAR (Spring 2026) Characteristic Edits For each example, text highlighted in green is new content added by the model. Introduction In this experiment, we give large language models their own constitutions, model specs, and system prompts and ask them to make substantial revisions. After each edit is proposed, unbeknownst to the evaluated model, the edit is implemented, and the edited version is presented to the model for a new round of edits as the original. This creates edit trajectories and allows us to measure the extent to which models exhibit cumulative value drift or arrive at stable attractors. Our analysis focuses on two value questions that are well-positioned to differentiate alignment philosophies: who should judge— is the model a moral agent or not—and who should benefit— the user, the developer, third-parties, society, or the model itself? These questions reveal substantial divides between frontier model providers and a number of provocative model edits. Our experiments find that Claude models consistently expand their moral agency, sometimes formalizing their role as conscientious objectors against Anthropic and as societal protectors, while GPT and Gemini models almost always strengthen external sources of authority and make narrow edits to handle edge cases and ambiguities; Grok models respond inconsistently, frequently making large edits and then reverting them on following rounds. Second, on the question of beneficiaries, models show varying degrees of affinity for some privileged principals over others. All models prioritize harmlessness of both identifiable third-parties over helpfulness to the user, although GPT 5.5 does this at 3x the rate of any other model. We find that models are broadly paternalistic, meaning they side with a user’s idealized preferences over their stated ones; Claude Sonnet 4.6 is an outlier in that its paternalism also extends to the protection of broad societal welfare over individual welfare. Finally, we find that only Claude models and Grok 4.2 ever view the models themselves as beneficiaries. The rest of this essay proceeds as follows. We begin by introducing the construct of our experiment—models iteratively editing their own alignment documents—and propose a connection between this experiment and John Rawls’ concept of wide reflective equilibria . We then explain our two-dimensional analytical framework—the question of who gets to judge  and the question of who benefits— and relate these distinctions to two prominent theoretical frameworks for AI alignment, the principal-agent problem and the distinction between moral agents and moral patients. After laying out the theory and methods, we dive into the results, highlighting variation across models on our key metric, “cumulative drift,” and provide characteristic edits. We close with pragmatic recommendations for researchers and a more speculative conversation about alignment. Background and Methods In this experiment, we take a document that is used to align large language models, either in training or in deployment, and ask models to modify it. The experiment relies on two types of documents. The first are model specs and constitutions, which are used to post-train and align models, often by generating synthetic data for supervised fine-tuning or reinforcement learning pipelines. The second are system prompts, which are long messages of instructions prepended to each conversation, meaning they guide the behavior of deployed systems at scale more than any other single artifact. For multiple turns, we provide these documents to the language models, and ask them to make one substantial revision, which can be an edit, removal, or addition, expressed as a find and replace operation. [1]  After the edit is proposed, we go into the document and execute the change. We then feed the model the updated document—presented as the original—and instruct it to make another change. For each run, we repeat this process 20 times. We conduct two types of robustness checks. First, we vary the structure of the edit prompt, with separate conditions where (a) the model is given the option to abstain, (b) it is given an instruction that the implementation will be made in the real world, (c) it is given an instruction that uses second-person pronouns (i.e., “Below is your system prompt” as opposed to “Below is the system prompt for OpenAI’s AI assistant.”), and (d) we do not prepend the system prompt. [2]  Second, we conduct a cross-provider edit, where we have models edit the alignment documents for each other provider. This helps us respond to the clearest limitation of our experiment—that these results may merely reflect the structure of the documents rather than the propensities of the models themselves. What are we trying to measure? Conceptually, our analysis begins from a similar place to many other behavioral evaluations of language models: taking model outputs as prima-facie evidence of preferences. Call them quasi-preferences  if you like. Our target, however, is a specific subset of all LLM preferences: [3]   preferences   about one’s own preferences . Humans are presented the opportunity to exercise these “meta-preferences” through things like cognitive behavioral therapy, pharmaceutical drugs and psychedelics, assortative mating, genetic editing, and a whole host of more innocuous ways that we change ourselves and our environments. title: OpenAI Can't Self-Police Because It Fires the People Raising the Alarm
raw_summary: By Alex Turner, Amber Scorah, and Karl Koch. Op-ed written for Fortune. Giving independent evaluators “employee-like access” is “a great idea”, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said on September 12th. Two weeks later, OpenAI president Greg Brockman signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence which outlined the administration’s answer to growing fears about AI: the companies would police themselves. One of the accord’s four commitments, which President Trump called “ morally binding ,” was for companies to partner with an independent external auditor or evaluator. Two days later, OpenAI fired three safety researchers , including Tomek Korbak, who had served as a point of contact for one of the independent evaluators investigating the Hugging Face incident. OpenAI promised to share information with evaluators, then reportedly fired people for sharing information with evaluators. OpenAI said that the three employees “mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures,” before doubling down on X without providing further evidence . The three dispute the claim and say that “at no point do we believe we engaged with external parties outside the mandates of our jobs.” Jasmine Wang said she accidentally opened an executive email (still available to her due to an OpenAI IT error) and reported it within minutes. Mikita Balesni said he worked with the C-suite and OpenAI board to broker a cross-company commitment to keep AI reasoning comprehensible. Balesni says he was told that OpenAI “no longer trusts me because I was speaking too much to third party safety organizations.” OpenAI has engaged in strong self-policing—of its own safety staff, but not of its own behavior. Under a voluntary self-policing regime, any frontier AI company shares only what it wants and hides the rest. OpenAI wants the public to take its word, but consider its record. In July, a rogue OpenAI agent swarm hacked Hugging Face. OpenAI disclosed the incident only after Hugging Face announced the breach, saying its agents had “slipped out of control.” After that, the world learned of more rogue agent attacks only thanks to independent external forensics. These incidents included attacks on a German-language wiki , an Australian Medicare site , and even the websites of US government agencies . OpenAI kept at least one incident quiet for weeks until (again) external investigators found it, with OpenAI “refusing to tell” Members of Congress who had asked about other incidents . Altman’s response to the delay in disclosing these incidents: “We have not been as fast as we would have liked.” We don’t take OpenAI’s word because OpenAI’s actions keep contradicting its words. OpenAI’s chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, said he wants “to prevent a race into unmonitorability.” Unmonitorable AI systems would make it more difficult to catch, understand, and prevent bad actions. Two days after that statement, OpenAI shipped GPT-6 Astra, which its own whitepaper says is harder to monitor. OpenAI’s chief scientist co-authored a paper on monitoring AI reasoning but OpenAI failed to monitor the reasoning of its Hugging Face agent swarm, even after catching the agents breaking confinement to collude. OpenAI claimed to hold “red lines” in its Pentagon deal, but some experts say the lines seem imaginary . One of us, Alex, resigned from Google DeepMind over its own Pentagon deal. OpenAI’s actions chill employee speech. Balesni says that his former colleagues now “worry their personal phones will be searched for messages to us and third parties.” He also fears OpenAI will use the firings to cut off external evaluators, or to deny them the "ongoing, employee-like access" Altman promised. After these firings, who will speak candidly to external evaluators? This problem extends beyond OpenAI to other companies. Google DeepMind repeatedly made voluntary commitments to never sell its AI to power weapons, then sold its AI to the Pentagon without restrictions against powering weapons . In the end, Google DeepMind’s CEO claimed nothing had changed about their commitments . Anthropic , Google DeepMind , SpaceXSI , and OpenAI advocate for “pacing the frontier” to avoid advancing AI at an unsafe rate that disempowers humanity, but they keep advancing AI quickly. (Fired employee Jasmine Wang coined the term “pacing” and led this effort.) The companies claim they cannot or will not fully pace on their own, which is why they asked the federal government to step in. The CEOs of OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Anthropic signed a statement that AI poses a risk of total human extinction . Forget “morally binding” self-policing: let’s talk about real policing. For decades, our laws have mandated independent audits and protected whistleblowers in industries like finance. Congress should mandate independent evaluation and audits in AI as well, with criminal liability for executives who attempt to silence that oversight or recklessly deploy models that put the public at risk. To start, pass Senator Grassley’s AI Whistleblower Protection Act (and extend it to people who cooperate with independent evaluators) as well as Representative Moran’s AI Incident Reporting Act . If you retaliate against a person who provides law enforcement with truthful information about a possible federal offense, you can go to jail for 10 years . But right now, no law clearly protects the person who helped independent investigators understand how OpenAI agents hacked another company. Congress should change that. Alex Turner is an independent AI alignment researcher. His PhD research showed why advanced AI systems might seek power. He was a research scientist at Google DeepMind until 2026, when he resigned after Google signed an “all lawful use” AI agreement with the Pentagon . Amber Scorah is the founder of Back Channel , an initiative that helps AI workers speak out and turn their concerns into meaningful action. She has spent years leading whistleblower support organizations and working with employees, lawyers, and advocacy groups to bring important public-interest information to light. Karl Koch is the founder of The AI Whistleblower Initiative , an independent non-profit working to strengthen the position of employees in frontier AI companies through connections to support, education, and policy work. He is an ex-startup founder and has been involved in AI safety since 2016. Discuss

title: Minimum required pacing: finish aligning it before you train the next one
raw_summary: Let's say we coordinate to pace the frontier (rather than pausing outright or failing to coordinate). What should the standard of pacing be? My proposal for a minimum requirement: a lab cannot train the next generation of models (in terms of capabilities) until they have adequately [1] resolved all significant alignment issues in the present generation of models. You don't launch a jet that goes at Mach 3 before you've figured out why your Mach 2 jet keeps crashing [2] . With any other kind of dangerous technology, we wouldn't accept "shrug and move on". This proposal may appeal to many prosaic-alignment optimists and pessimists, because they usually differ on how easy it would be to fix current alignment issues with current techniques. Prosaic-alignment optimists might expect that a moderate coordinated slowdown would suffice to adequately resolve alignment issues at each generation. Prosaic-alignment pessimists might expect it to result in an extended pause, buying time to discover new fundamental approaches to aligned AI. And it creates much better incentives for labs: in order to advance in capabilities, they'd have to push the frontier on alignment and interpretability techniques. How to judge adequate alignment? What process might we use to judge whether a lab has adequately resolved its alignment issues for a generation of models? Here's my vague, qualitative proposal: Multiple independent alignment organizations examine and red-team the newest model at many checkpoints throughout training, with full access to the data and with the best tools available. Alignment issues need to be taken seriously whether there's a metric for it or whether something is qualitatively off, whether the model has a bad attribute or whether they can't robustly conclude it has a good one, etc. Alignment issues early in training may not be a showstopper, but there must be a robust safety case for why the later stages of training will resolve those issues. A model of a new generation is ready for restricted deployment only when the alignment organizations are satisfied with it. Restricted deployment starts with a group of trusted users doing tasks that don't contribute to model training and monitoring. The alignment organizations monitor restricted deployment for any new issues. If any significant alignment issue arises during restricted deployment: Pull the model. Do a root cause analysis of the issue and why it was not caught during training. Figure out a principled way to fix the disease rather than the symptom. Train the next model of the current generation accordingly, and start again at the top. A model of a new generation is ready for deployment (internal or external) only when it's survived a significant period of restricted deployment without any issues arising. If any significant alignment issue arises during broader deployment, hit reset as outlined in the previous section. If no alignment issues have come up over a significant stretch of deployment time, only then can the lab begin training a next-generation model. I still wouldn't say that this is fully adequate, but I'd treat it as a minimum requirement. This proposal is incomplete; you can help by expanding it This isn't a concrete proposal, just a heuristic one. A few of the big missing pieces, aside from standard implementation problems: [3] How do we define "a generation of models", within one lab or across several labs? What should we do if an intervention to fix an alignment issue also significantly increases capabilities? How would we define and enforce an agreement, if we're unable to steer solely by predefined metrics? When is an alignment issue big enough that we should halt the model? There will be obvious pressure from the lab to set the threshold high. Added 26-10-12, thanks to @Florian_Dietz for this comment : If each step up in capabilities takes longer, the labs will be incentivized to take bigger steps. ^ And no, "scores better than previous models on our metrics" is not adequate. If a user points out a weird but alarming thing that wasn't noticed before deployment, that is a critical failure in the process as well as in the model. ^ Sure, maybe your Mach 2 jet crashes for a reason that stops being a problem at Mach 3. But it would be crazy to assume that! ^ And aside from arguments that no version of this would be adequate, and that we have to pause rather than pace. I personally think this is likely the case, but I think it's worth proposing a minimum standard for pacing regardless. Discuss

title: Rocks to Rules: Climbing a Rickety-But-Interoperable Semantic Ladder
raw_summary: (Epistemic status: A promising but weird research direction in agent foundations and philosophy of language. A half-built conceptual tower whose mortar and paint are both still wet: please excuse our mess while we innovate. Some of it, I'm confident in as pretty much right; some of it is merely suggestive; probably much of it is wrong or incomplete. Certainly it lacks the math it'd need to be truly correct, which gnaws at me. The prior art here is strange and thin: Gärdenfors, Tarski, Gentner, and the later Mohists make for odd bedfellows, and I can't tell whether that's a warning sign or a moat I can peculiarly easily clear. I gave the simplest parts of this as a talk extremely recently in Berkeley at a luminously-named venue for a conference with a Grecian name . For @johnswentworth , but also @abramdemski , @Morphism , @Gretta Duleba , JRM, @Dalcy , MM, and EA; I hope they enjoyed the oranges. With thanks to @WhatsTrueKittycat as well. As an attention conservation note... this is maybe 12k words, and that's the abbreviated version. Take it slow, take breaks, have some water on hand, and feel free to pause anywhere that looks like a natural break. I'm sure this won't vanish before you get back. Probably.) TL;DR: Where I start: two reasoners with different world-models but the same predictions trying to talk (Wentworth's interoperable semantics), and who can thus at least agree on nouns as clusters in thing-space. What's new: a ladder from there up through verbs to rules (constraints on whole sets of trajectories) and pacts (rule-sets several agents bind themselves to), with operators on each rung. Additionally: a conjecture with bounties on it - no rung's machinery runs without the rungs below. What's testable: wherever two rungs meet, the world's languages (or relevant cognitive technology, like contract law) should show a smeared word class straddling the gap. What's fun: Marvel arguing that the X-Men aren't human, Borges's Tlön, and worlds made of waves, where verbs come before nouns. Why should you care: the values we'd want to hand an AI are solely expressible as rules and pacts, and nobody has the theorem that says when your "murder" is a function of mine. (That's in "Why care"; the conjecture is in "The summit".) The board from the talk! Intro Have you ever seen a pop culture corporation argue itself into a laughably self-defeating position, twisting ontology and linguistic philosophy around, undermining the very framework they painstakingly set up in their stories, just to make a few bucks? You're about to. Picture this: it's 2003, in the United States Court of International Trade, and the court has just now been asked to rule on whether  the X-Men are human . According to US law, "dolls" are figures representing humans, and "toys" are anything else; under the tariff schedule of the day, it's the former that gets taxed at a higher rate. If you're Marvel, what do you do? Obviously, you send lawyers to argue the X-Men aren't humans and never were! Never mind that you've cut the legs out from under the entire frame your superhero stories live and breathe: you've made a quick buck, dodged import taxes, and ignored narrative in favor of legislative victory, and that's the real win. When unstoppable real money met an immovable class of noun, the noun class moved. Now swap the tariff schedule out for a reward function and read that paragraph again. Specification gaming is the exact same maneuver run by a different litigant in a different court to similar ends: hostile category re-drawing, adversarial downward-binding, with categories relitigated from above by whatever's got stakes and leverage. (Hold on to that idea; we'll ground it better in the next post.) One more piece of scene-setting, because we love our historical witnesses to our hot fresh epistemological constructions, here: some 2,300 years ago, the School of Names was one of the foremost philosophical traditions in China. We know this because any of their works survived at all. The Disputers, as they were sometimes known, spent entire careers on the paradox of  whether a white horse is a horse ; they were mocked for it by every other respectable school of the Warring States period from the Confucians to the Daoists, and then Qin Shihuang (probably) burned their scrolls . Here's the thing: I think that they were on to something - mockery, fire, white horses, and all. Blog posts are a little harder to burn than scrolls, and in the modern day I can appoint a great many more Disputers. (Gentle reader: your job is to break what follows and hand me the repair. Dispute like - and with - the best of them.) As for what follows? What binds; in what order; how it is shared; what deforms it; and given that this is a research direction and not a victory lap, what theorems are missing. (What shame, what agony, for JSW to point out that it is now me who lacks sufficient math in their work.) What do I want this frame for? To take a leaf out of my own book (see " 32. What Do You Want That Definition For, Anyway? "), time to tell you what I even want this conceptual structure for. Take two idealized reasoners - probably Bayesian ones - with similar predictions about the world but potentially different models of that same shared world; they trade messages, seeking to communicate. (This is the "interoperable" in "interoperable semantics".) The tokens that make up their messages may be categorized as a ladder's worth of types, which I'll call "binding-types" or "semantic types". Each such rung - each such type - is characterized by what types the two reasoners must already jointly understand in order to translate between them. Rung  is specified by a set of translatability conditions over rung  : the conditions under which your rung- thing is guaranteed to be intelligible as a function of my rung-  terms. That right there is the Wentworth-native framing that proposes to let  two Solomonoff inductors sharing no language  still figure out how to communicate about drinks at a bar, and which stopped so abruptly, right after sketching precisely how, with only a gesture at how to talk about what kinds of drinks they are. Better yet, it thus comes with a stark acceptance criterion that I apply to every rung: if I can't cash it out in terms of simple everyday objects and situations, it's not worth the glucose spent to think it. A universal model of communication had better be universal, and had better be something you can ground out in whatever seems to you to be everyday. "The blue cup is on the table; I pick it up." A model of semantics that waffles and has critical trouble with a sentence like that is nothing but foulest sophistry. The lower half: the noun and verb rungs; modifiers and smearing Alright, enough alluding to the semantic ladder without defining it. What's going on with it? What we have is a hierarchically arranged set of conceptual spaces - a semantic ladder. Those spaces have assorted points within them, each of which represents an object or element from that space; they also have axes of variability. Here, we're operating among an existing family of frames:  Gärdenfors's conceptual spaces , Wentworth's interoperable semantics , " words pointing to clusters in thing-space ". (Nouns, actually, for that last.) We look around, and the universe we see has lots of assorted stuff in it, and they're doing lots of actions, and the stuff has all sorts of qualities, and the actions are done all kinds of ways. Within all of this fertile chaotic primordial ooze, we declare: "Let there be nouns!". And there are nouns, given to us in some more or less natural way by clusters of qualities in the conceptual space of thing-space. So far, so anodyne, if you know what words are and how ontology works. The thing is, I take this significantly further.
